title: Genesis ends (Genesis 49–50)
hook: Jacob's blessings, Joseph's forgiveness, and a coffin waiting to go home; finishing a book, the synagogue says "be strong"
tomorrow: a king who knew not Joseph

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ephraim, Jacob's crossed hands, and a blessing parents still say on Friday night. Your line was may you be like them. Today, the last page of the first book. Day seventy-six.

A synagogue on a Saturday morning in winter. The Torah scroll lies open on the table, and the reader is chanting the very last verse of Genesis. The whole book, from let there be light to here, is about to be finished. And the moment the last word is sung, the whole room stands up and calls out together, three words, loud: chazak, chazak, venitchazek. Be strong, be strong, and let us strengthen one another. It's a little like the cheer at the end of a long race. Today: how the book ends, and why people shout.
screen: `THE LAST VERSE OF GENESIS.` → `THE WHOLE ROOM STANDS.` → `CHAZAK, CHAZAK, VENITCHAZEK.`

segments.voice: Jacob gathers his twelve sons and blesses them one by one. The blessings are honest; some are praise, some are hard words about old wrongs. Then he asks to be buried with his fathers in the cave of Machpelah, in Canaan, and he dies. Joseph and his brothers carry him home, with a great Egyptian procession, and bury him. And then, walking back to Egypt, the brothers get scared. Maybe now that Father is gone, Joseph will pay us back. They send him a message, and they fall down before him. And Joseph weeps, and says: "Fear not; for am I in the place of God? And as for you, ye meant evil against me; but God meant it for good." He'll take care of them, and their little ones. Years of peace after the reunion, and they still needed to hear it again. Sometimes forgiveness has to be said twice. Then Joseph grows old, and he asks one thing: when God brings you out of here, carry my bones with you. And Genesis ends with this line: "and he was put in a coffin in Egypt." The book that began with a garden ends with a coffin in a foreign land, waiting to go home. That's where the chazak comes in. Chazak means be strong. The tradition says it at the end of every one of the five books of the Torah, and it makes sense here most of all. We've finished something long. The ending isn't tidy. And the next book begins in slavery. So before you turn the page: be strong, be strong, and strengthen each other.
screen: `JACOB BLESSES TWELVE SONS.` · `AM I IN THE PLACE OF GOD?` · `A COFFIN IN EGYPT.` · `CHAZAK: BE STRONG.` · then, large: `YE MEANT EVIL; GOD MEANT IT FOR GOOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: finish one small thing, and say chazak. Settle, and breathe. Think of something small you've left undone. A drawer, an email, a chapter of a book, a thank-you note, a dish in the sink. Choose it. When the bell ends, go and finish it. And when it's done, say the word, even quietly: chazak. Be strong. Look back, too, at this part of the path: Rachel's grave, the coat, the pit, Tamar, the prison, the dreams, the cup, Judah, Ani Yosef, the grandsons. You finished it. The bell holds the time.
Chazak. Be strong. Called out in synagogue when a book of the Torah is finished: chazak, chazak, venitchazek.
Your line: be strong, be strong. Today, when you finish anything, even something small, say chazak, and tell someone else the same. Day seventy-six.

howItsDone: When the reading of each of the five books of the Torah is completed in synagogue, the congregation stands and calls out chazak, chazak, venitchazek, and the reader repeats it.

fork.setup: you're Joseph. your father has died, and your brothers fall before you, afraid you'll finally take revenge. what do you do?
fork.reveal: he weeps and says, "Fear not; for am I in the place of God?" and promises to care for them and their little ones.

original.note: Hebrew: be strong. the same root describes the hardening of Pharaoh's heart later in Exodus.

trapdoor: what you thought: chazak is a cheer.
what it means: be strong, be strong, and let us strengthen one another, said together when a book of the Torah is finished.
what a scholar hears: an old synagogue custom; it echoes Joshua 1, where God tells Joshua to be strong and of good courage.

notes: 'Seventeen years of peace': Jacob lived 17 years in Egypt (47:28). Confirm.
Chazak custom: congregation calls it out and the reader repeats it; Sephardi practice differs somewhat (e.g. chazak u-varuch at an aliyah). Confirm framing.
Link of chazak custom to Joshua 1 offered as an echo, not an origin. Confirm.
This day closes the Joseph part (days 64–76); the practice names the part's days.

Editor review: hook no longer opens with 'Picture'; burial place corrected to the cave of Machpelah (Genesis 49:30 and 50:13 name Machpelah and Mamre, not Hebron) in teach and match; 'seventeen years' cut (it comes from 47:28, outside the day's cited text).
